14_marg1035: BEDE. 'Anaglypha' in Greek are called 'celaturae', carvings, in Latin, because to the works of the virtues which the Church exercises throughout the world in holy and perfect men, those above all to whom the care of the faithful is committed and the keys of the kingdom of heaven given ought to apply themselves with all diligence, that as much as they are above the rest in rank so much they may excel in the merit of good action. For they have on themselves the figure of the cherubim carved when they imitate in mind and work, as far as they can, the angelic life on earth. They have figures of palm trees when they meditate with fixed intention on the heavenly retribution; for the palm is the adornment of the victor's hand. They have carvings very much projecting when they show to all most certain proofs of good works, which no one can interpret amiss. And all these are covered with golden plates when, beyond the other flowers of the virtues, the brightness of love shines preeminent in the great members of the Church. To these little doors a veil was added, as is written in Paralipomenon: "He made also a veil," it says, "of violet, purple, scarlet, and silk: and wrought cherubims in it." For the sake of beauty, namely, that among the gilded walls silk too might shine, but in the same signification as the little doors. It was hung before the ark and the entrance of the oracle, that, as the little doors were opened at fitting hours, so the veil too might be drawn back for those coming who entered into the holy of holies. The careful drawing back of this veil, then, signifies the opening of the law and of the heavenly kingdom which was given us through the incarnation of Christ. Whence when the Lord was baptized the heavens were opened, to show that through the baptism which he consecrated for us we must enter the gate of heaven; and when he died on the cross likewise "the veil was rent in the midst from the top even to the bottom," showing that the figures of the law were now ended, and the truth of the gospel and the heavenly secrets, and the very entrance of heaven, were no longer to be prophesied and signified figuratively, but to be opened at once to all who from the beginning of the world up to that time had passed from the world in the faith of truth. For on the fortieth day after the Lord's resurrection all sought heaven with him, and, every veil removed, received many mansions in the Father's house according to their merits. For us too, who were yet to be, the entrance was unbarred in that same hour, but only through inward desires of inward goods, through faith and the sacraments of the Lord's passion, through the fervour of sincere love, through the mortification of the concupiscence of the flesh, and through the daily help of the angels. Whence that same veil, under which one entered into the oracle, was made of violet, purple, scarlet and silk, and cherubims were woven into it. For violet, which imitates the colour of the sky, is compared to the desires of heavenly things. Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and displays a bloody hue, signifies the sacrament of the Lord's passion, which we must imitate by carrying our cross. In the scarlet of red colour is expressed the virtue of love, of which it is said: "Was not our heart burning within us" of Jesus "whilst he spoke to us in the way" etc. Silk, which springs green from the earth and by the long labour of craftsmen puts off its native greenness and is brought to whiteness, suggests the chastisement of the flesh, whose inborn moisture, as it were, the Apostle bids to be dried up, saying: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness" etc. And to what grace of whiteness he would have it brought he shows elsewhere, saying: "I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God" etc. Cherubims are woven in and made with the same colours when, in all that we do piously, we are protected by the Lord's gift from the poisoned darts of the demons through the guard of the angels. Cherubims are woven in when, in the good things we do, we use the multitude of knowledge unceasingly, looking always to the divine words, and, lest perhaps we stray from the path of the virtues, rule our steps continually by beholding them.
14_marg1036: As the entrance of the oracle, by which one came to the ark of the Lord and the cherubims, signifies 'the entrance of heaven', by which we desire to be brought to the vision of God and of the heavenly citizens, so the entrance into the temple [signifies] the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter into the present Church. This designates our entrance to faith, that one to hope. Whence the posts of this entrance are foursquare, on account of the four books of the gospel, by whose teaching we are instructed in the faith of truth.
14_marg1037: BEDE. Foursquare, namely on account of the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance, on which, as on a most firm foundation, the whole structure of good acts rests. For prudence is that by which we learn what we should do and how it befits us to live. Fortitude, that by which we fulfil what we have learned is to be done; these the prophet briefly embraces, saying: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?" Light, namely, that he may teach what we ought to do; salvation, that he may strengthen us to do it. Temperance is that by which we discern, lest we give ourselves more or less than is just to prudence and fortitude. And because whoever uses prudence, fortitude and temperance is truly just, justice follows fourth after prudence, fortitude and temperance.
14_interl1398: the love of God and of neighbour
14_marg1038: Because they look toward one another, so that the one cannot be had without the other: the outer door is brotherly love, the inner divine, because the former is first in time, the latter higher in dignity, and through the former one enters the latter; for in the love of neighbour one learns how the creator ought to be loved.
14_marg1039: BEDE. Because in each love two things are chiefly to be observed. In the love of God, the faith of truth and purity of working: "For without faith it is impossible to please God," and: "Faith without works is dead." In the love of brotherhood, patience and kindness. Whence: "Charity is patient, is kind," that is, that it may forgive the injuries of neighbours and do good to them. Whence: "Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you." This love we desire to be spent on us, saying: "Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors."
14_marg1040: Each door was opened holding one another, because the virtues are joined and cannot be separated; for neither faith without works nor works without faith please, nor does it suffice to bear injuries for one who does not impart necessaries to him whom he bears with, nor to supply necessaries for one who does not know how to forgive from the heart the troubles brought upon him. For the opening of the doors does not signify a separation of the virtues, but that through their joining the entrance of the Church lies open to us more and more, that the more we abound in them the more truly we may be joined to the companies of the saints; just as the dividing of the Red Sea, by which the people of God escaped the pursuing Egyptian, signified not a division of baptism but an opening, by which, all sins being extinguished, we pass over to the shore and firm ground of the virtues.
14_marg1041: BEDE. It is to be noted that in the entrance of the oracle there are said to have been two doors, but not double; but in the entrance of the temple, that is, of the former house, there were two doors such that each was double, because in the present Church it is needful for us to enter and lead such a life that we keep the love of God and neighbour through faith and working, through patience and kindness. But in the future life, where we shall see God and our neighbours in the light of eternal beatitude, we shall enjoy the same twofold love without labour but in the highest sweetness. Whence the entrance of the inner house had two doors, but single. For faith is not necessary there, where we shall see openly what we now believe and hope; nor the labour of works, because we shall be given the perpetual wage of what we labour at here; nor patience, where there is nothing adverse; nor the bounty of kindness, where there is no need.
14_marg1042: According to the form of the work it was provided, for the sake of beauty, that in the same entrance of the temple there should be two doors. For it was necessary that the walls of the house, which had a hundred and twenty cubits in height, should also have some cubits of thickness; at the outer edge of this thickness the doors were fixed, so that each door was level with the wall, and whether one stood within or without the temple and looked at the door, it should seem to him in every way one wall. Likewise the cedar wall, since it was twenty cubits in length and height, had no small thickness. Therefore in its entrance too two doors were made, that on each side, that is, within and without, the door might show level with the wall. And since the door and the wall had the same figures, so that it might seem one wall stretched out in every way and continuously, the one displaying [the grace] of beauty, the other prefiguring the dispensation of a mystery.
14_marg1043: Or the door which held together is opened when by the ministry of the preacher it is discerned what properly belongs to the knowledge of faith and what to chastity of living, which two cannot be separated; and that it is little to bear the evils of neighbours and not to bestow good things on them, since these are most surely wont to abide indissolubly in the hearts of the perfect.
14_marg1044: These things have been explained above, because on the walls of the house and on the inner doors the same figures or carvings were made, because the same mysteries of faith, hope and charity which the lofty and perfect grasp loftily, and which all the elect perceive fully in the eternal vision, are also handed on to the rude who are to be catechized, to be learned and confessed according to each one's capacity, that, initiated into the sacred mysteries, they may at length come to grasp what they have believed.
14_marg1045: AND HE BUILT THE INNER COURT etc. BEDE. Of the inner court he speaks briefly; of the outer he seems to be altogether silent; but in the Words of the Days [Paralipomenon] mention is made of both, where it is written: "He made also the court of the priests, and a great hall, and doors in the hall, which he covered with brass." Now the inner court, which is called the priests' because the priests and Levites ministered in it, surrounded the temple on every side; but on the east, whence was the entrance of the temple, it was set apart much farther from the temple than on the other three sides, because on that side, that is, before the face of the temple, the ministries of the holy things were done. There was the brazen altar for offering victims to the Lord, there the ten lavers for washing them, there the brazen sea was placed for washing the hands and feet of the priests when they went in to minister. And this court had three cubits of height, as Josephus relates, to keep the rest from the entrance of the temple and signify that this was lawful for the priests alone. And it had a gate on the eastern side, up to which the people brought their victims and sacrifices to be received by the priests and carried to the altar. Of the outer court, which the Words of the Days call the great hall, Josephus wrote thus: "Outside this temple he built another hall made in a four-cornered figure, raising very great and broad porches and setting in it high and ample gates toward the four parts of the world, each of which faced toward its own wind at the four corners, where he placed golden doors." And a little after: "Into this sanctuary, then, all the people entered in whom was purification and the observance of the legal ordinances." These porches Cassiodorus, in the picture of the temple which he set on a wall, as he mentions in the exposition of the psalms, distinguished in a threefold order: setting the first order outside the court of the priests on every side in a square; the second in the same way outside the inmost porches, turned round about on every side; the outermost likewise on every side around the former porches. And so the temple was fortified on every side by a threefold defence of buildings, a pavement of marble being made under the open sky between the several buildings, and the inner walls of the houses, that is, those which looked toward the temple, being made solid on the outer columns. And so it came about that the whole structure of the temple was reasonably distinguished by variety of degrees. For the high priest entered into the holy of holies; into the temple itself the priests, [unclear in the edition: "purificari et non purificati"], together with the Levites and singers; into the inmost court of the greater hall the purified Jewish men, standing and praying under the open sky if it was fair, and if stormy betaking themselves into the nearest porches; into the outer court the purified Jewish women; into the outermost court the gentiles, and Jews who had lately come from the gentiles, up to the sixth day of purification. These things, as we found them distinguished in the picture of Cassiodorus, we have briefly noted, judging that he learned them from the ancient Jews, and that so learned a man would not have wished to set forth as an example for readers what he had not first known to be true. These places are recalled by the psalm of the last of the gradual psalms, which begins thus: "Behold now bless ye the Lord, all ye servants of the Lord: who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God." In these porches Jeremias and the other prophets, in these the Lord and the apostles preached. In one of these the Lord was sitting teaching when, the Pharisees tempting him, the woman was brought to him [unclear in the edition: "ad vitam iudicanda"]. In these he found those selling sheep and oxen and doves, whom he cast out of the temple. In these Peter and John, finding the lame man, healed him and, going in with him, led him further in to pray. In these the whole multitude of the people was praying when the angel appeared to Zachary as he offered incense at the altar of incense and taught him fully of the birth of the Lord's forerunner.
14_marg1046: But these courts with their porches could not hide the sight of the temple from those looking at it from afar, because the place in which the temple was was much higher than where the porches were. For as Josephus wrote: "The outermost structures of the courts, though raised to four hundred cubits, yet did not reach to the top of the mount on which the temple was built." These things about the structure of the temple we have thought should be made known to the studious reader. But in those things which sacred Scripture thought fit to relate let us seek the figures of mysteries; the rest let us use simply for knowledge of the history.
14_marg1047: The building of the temple within the court of the priests, then, expresses the life of the perfect in the Church, who by excellence of virtues draw near to the Lord and show to others the guidance of salvation by word and work. For a priest, sacerdos, is so called because he affords sacred guidance, sacrum ducatum, to the lesser; by which name are counted not only the ministers of the altar, namely bishops and presbyters, but also all who excel in loftiness of doctrine and conversation and profit not themselves only but many, who, while they present "their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God," spiritually exercise the priestly ministry. Whence Peter says to the whole Church: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people." And to the ancient people it is said: "You shall be to me a priestly kingdom, and a holy nation."
14_marg1048: But the great hall which was outside the court of the priests, in which all the people were wont to pray or hear the word, figures the life and manners of the carnal in the Church, to whom the Apostle says: "I could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal" etc. These are well signified by the great hall, because the number of such in the Church is much greater than that of the perfect. But as much as they surpass in number, so much they fall short in merit. Whence this hall holds very many, yet does not admit them into the inner parts of the gilded temple, nor to the office of the altar, nor into the court of the priests itself; because the carnal and the weak, though for the merit of chaste faith and piety they belong to the lot of the elect, are yet far from being made equal to those who say with confidence: "I dare not to speak of any of those things which Christ worketh not by me, for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed," and: "I have fought a good fight" etc.
14_marg1049: The common people came up to the court of the priests and brought their victims to the gate, and followed with their eyes the victims received by the priests and offered on the altar. Into the temple itself too, when it was opened, they looked from afar, and yet could not enter even the court of the priests. But from the lower places they cried to the Lord, because the simplicity of the carnal in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer what vows of piety they can. For they look from afar into the temple of the Lord when they rejoice to learn and admire the life of the lofty, and embrace with the affection of devout veneration those whom they cannot follow by imitation of virtue. They see the victims of the priests consumed on the altar by the sacred fire, because they know that the great works of the great are graciously accepted by the Lord through the Spirit.
14_marg1050: They bring their victims to the court of the priests, to be offered to the Lord through them, when, doing what good they can, they are strengthened by the exhortation of their elders and the more learned and commended by their intercession. They also offer victims to the priests, commending them to the Lord through them, when they give the needy saints the necessaries in which they abound, with a view to the reward. Whence: "Amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward." And so the same fire consumes the victims of both on the altar of God, when the Lord judges the alms of the rich, together with the great virtues of the saints, worthy of his regard and recompense. The multitude of believers, then, who, having left their possessions, served God with one heart and one soul, is itself the temple of God and the place within the court of the priests specially consecrated to him. But the great hall, and those praying in it round about the court of the priests, figure those who in their time believed from among the gentiles in Syria and in Antioch and the other provinces and cities, on whom the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem laid no more burden than that they abstain "from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication." By whose offerings, however, they wished the poor among the saints who were at Jerusalem to be supported, that, ministering carnal things to them, they might become partakers of their spiritual things. But Barnabas and Paul with their companions, who received their offerings and carried them to Jerusalem, are the priests who, receiving the victims, bring them to the altar of the Lord to be consecrated, because they brought the gifts of their devotion to the saints, who would pray for them. The court, then, set between the place of the people and of the priests, signifies that division which sets apart the carnal in the Church, and those lately beginning, from the citadel of the perfect, not by the lot of election but by the measure of merits. For the carnal believe it suffices them if they have faith, hope and charity and purity of works. The perfect, over and above all these, labour in preaching the word, give all they have to the poor, give themselves to vigils, fasts, hymns, spiritual canticles and sacred discourses, bear persecutions and dangers for justice' sake, and carry out with ready devotion of mind the other things which Paul glories that he did. Whence it follows: HE BUILT THE INNER COURT WITH THREE ROWS OF STONES etc.

14_interl1401: namely by good working without the corruption of pretence, without the addition of which faith, hope and charity cannot be true
14_marg1051: The one row of cedar beams is good working, shown without the corruption of pretence, without the addition of which faith, hope and charity cannot be true. For cedar wood, on account of the grace of its fragrance and the incorruptible power of its nature, designates the perseverance and good fame of devout action. Up to this court all the elect ascend who seek to please God by faith, hope, charity and work. This the perfect pass beyond by the lofty grace of merits when they advance to such a height of virtues that they can say to their hearers: "Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ," and: "Know you not that we shall judge angels? how much more things of this world?"
14_marg1052: BEDE. It is asked how the house of the Lord is said to have been finished in the eighth month in all its work and in all its vessels, when in what follows it is read that its dedication was completed in the seventh month. Nor is it credible that Solomon, building the temple for seven years, finished it in the eighth month of the eighth year, or put off the dedication of the finished [house] to the seventh month of the ninth year. Whence it seems rather likely that the house was built in seven years and seven months, so that the dedication was celebrated in that same seventh month, and on the twenty-third day of that month, according to Paralipomenon, Solomon sent the people away to their tents; and so, after one week, when the eighth month came, the house of the Lord was finished, namely all its works, the dedication itself having been completed before. Unless perhaps it is to be thought that after the temple was dedicated some vessels were added for its ministries up to the beginning of the eighth month, the king hastening so as to dedicate the temple wholly in the seventh month, which was all solemn; and so both are found true: that the temple was finished in the eighth month in all its work and vessels, and that it was dedicated in the seventh month.
14_marg1053: But that the house was finished in all its work in the eighth year and its eighth month pertains to the world to come and the day of judgment, when the Church shall come to such perfection that nothing can be found to be added to it. For then Christ will show us the Father, and it will suffice us. Now the day of judgment is expressed typically by the number eight, because it follows this world, which runs in seven days. Whence David entitled a psalm 'for the octave', which he sang for fear of the judgment, saying: "O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor chastise me in thy wrath."
14_marg1054: Because the Church is built of elect souls through the whole time of this world, which is run through in the circuit of seven days, and at the end of the world brings its growth to an end. Or for the signification of spiritual grace, through which alone the Church receives [the power] to be the Church; because without the gifts of the Spirit no one can be made faithful, or keep the faith, or by the merit of faith come to the crown of justice.
